title: Uppy 6.0 and Resumable File Uploads
summary: Set up resumable file uploads with Uppy and Tus, explore Uppy 6.0 changes to S3 signing and core packages, and check key migration steps from version 5.
body_markdown:
Uppy is an open-source JavaScript file uploader. Paired with its` @uppy/tus` plugin, it resumes large uploads after a dropped connection or a closed tab, so the user doesn’t have to send the file again from the start.


Most teams reach for a library after the same bug report: someone on hotel Wi-Fi reached 90% of a 2 GB video, the connection dropped, and the upload went back to zero. If you built your own uploader from our guides on[building a file upload dropzone](https://blog.openreplay.com/build-file-upload-dropzone/) or[custom file upload in React](https://blog.openreplay.com/custom-file-upload-react/) , this is the point where that approach stops being enough.


This article covers why resumable uploads matter, a minimal Uppy setup, what changed in Uppy 6.0, and how much work the upgrade from 5.x takes.


## Key Takeaways


- Tus is an open protocol, built on HTTP, that makes uploads resumable. A dropped connection or a closed tab doesn’t lose progress: the upload carries on from the last byte the server received.
- Uppy 6.0 rewrites` @uppy/aws-s3` around three signing modes (` getCredentials` ,` signRequest` and` companionEndpoint` ), and each configuration uses exactly one of them.
- In Uppy 6.0,` @uppy/utils` ,` @uppy/store-default` ,` @uppy/companion-client` and` @uppy/provider-views` now ship inside` @uppy/core` as subpath exports.
- Projects that use the` uppy` meta-package or the CDN bundle need few or no code changes to move to 6.0.
- Self-hosted Companion must be upgraded to Companion 7 before the client moves to` @uppy/core` 6, because OAuth tokens now travel over Companion’s WebSocket. Companion 7 also runs on Express 5.


## Why Use Uppy Instead of a Hand-Rolled Uploader?


A hand-rolled uploader built on a single` fetch` or` XMLHttpRequest` POST can’t pick up where it left off. When the connection drops, all the bytes already sent are lost.[Tus](https://tus.io/) solves this at the protocol level: the client asks the server how much it already has, then sends only the rest. Session replay makes the cost of not having this easy to see: after a failed upload, you can watch the user go back to the file picker and choose the same large file again.


Tus resumable uploads do need a server-side counterpart. The[@uppy/tus docs](https://uppy.io/docs/tus/) recommend` tusd` , and Tus servers can store files locally or in external storage such as S3.


## Minimal Uppy Setup with Dashboard and Tus


Three packages give you a complete resumable uploader:` @uppy/core` holds the state,` @uppy/dashboard` provides the UI, and` @uppy/tus` handles the transfer.


```text
import   Uppy   from   '  @uppy/core  '  ;
import   Dashboard   from   '  @uppy/dashboard  '  ;
import   Tus   from   '  @uppy/tus  '  ;
import   '  @uppy/core/css/style.min.css  '  ;
import   '  @uppy/dashboard/css/style.min.css  '  ;


new   Uppy  ()
.  use  (  Dashboard  , {   inline  :   true  ,   target  :   '  body  '   })
// Point this at your own tus server, e.g. a tusd instance
.  use  (  Tus  , {   endpoint  :   '  https://your-tus-server/files/  '   });
```


` inline: true` renders the Dashboard straight into the target element instead of opening it as a modal. If you would rather build your own progress UI, our article on building an[upload progress bar](https://blog.openreplay.com/build-upload-progress-bar-js/) covers the underlying events.


Remote sources such as Google Drive go through Companion, Uppy’s server component. Companion fetches the file on the server, so the bytes never pass through the user’s browser. One detail matters here: the` chunkSize` setting in` @uppy/tus` only covers files sent from the user’s device. Uploads that go through Companion follow Companion’s own` chunkSize` setting, so set both if you need a size limit on each request.


By default,` @uppy/tus` retries a failed chunk after a series of delays and limits how many uploads run at the same time. When the server returns HTTP 429, its default` onShouldRetry` logic pauses all queued requests and waits before trying again, stepping through the delays in` retryDelays` .


## What’s New in Uppy 6.0


Uppy 6.0 has three headline changes:` @uppy/aws-s3` is rewritten from scratch, four support packages are merged into` @uppy/core` , and` @uppy/instagram` is removed. According to the[Uppy 6.0 release post](https://uppy.io/blog/uppy-6.0/) , six packages received a major version bump:` @uppy/core` ,` @uppy/companion` ,` @uppy/aws-s3` ,` @uppy/tus` ,` @uppy/components` and` uppy` .


In Uppy 5, the old` @uppy/aws-s3` plugin had up to eight callbacks, and the set you needed changed with your setup: multipart or single upload, with Companion or without, signing in the browser or on a server. The rewrite replaces all of that with three[signing modes](https://uppy.io/docs/aws-s3/) , and you pick exactly one:


Mode Where signing happens Companion needed


` getCredentials` In the browser (SigV4), using temporary credentials from your endpoint No


` signRequest` Your own signer No


` companionEndpoint` Companion Yes


```text
import   Uppy   from   '  @uppy/core  '  ;
import   AwsS3   from   '  @uppy/aws-s3  '  ;


new   Uppy  ().  use  (  AwsS3  , {
// Swap this for an R2, MinIO or Spaces endpoint
s3Endpoint  :   '  https://my-bucket.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com  '  ,
region  :   '  eu-west-1  '  ,
getCredentials  :   async   ()   =>   fetch  (  '  /s3-credentials  '  ).  then  ((  r  )   =>   r  .  json  ()),
});
```


Companion is no longer required to upload to S3. With` getCredentials` , the browser signs each request itself, and the plugin works with any S3-compatible service, including Cloudflare R2, MinIO and DigitalOcean Spaces. The` @uppy/aws-s3` reference lists the fields` getCredentials` must return, so in the example above your` /s3-credentials` endpoint has to send back that exact shape. The release post also says the rewrite closed long-standing bugs in retry backoff, credential expiry, offline detection and pausing or resuming multipart uploads. The plugin’s CI tests now run against a real MinIO server rather than mocks.


## How Do You Upgrade from Uppy 5 to 6?


If you use the` uppy` meta-package or the CDN bundle, the 6.0 upgrade needs few or no code changes. Everyone else should work through this list, and the[official migration guide](https://github.com/transloadit/uppy.io/blob/main/docs/guides/migration-guides.md#migrate-from-uppy-5x-to-6x) has the full details:


- **Individual packages:** move imports from` @uppy/utils` ,` @uppy/store-default` ,` @uppy/companion-client` and` @uppy/provider-views` to their` @uppy/core` subpaths. The old packages are deprecated on npm.
- **Self-hosted Companion:** upgrade to Companion 7 first, then move the client to` @uppy/core` 6. Companion 7 still supports older Uppy clients, but an Uppy 6 client won’t work with Companion 6 or older. Companion 7 is built on Express 5 and won’t work as middleware in an Express 4 app, so move your app to Express 5 before you switch.` companion.socket()` now needs` companionOptions` as its second argument. Hosted Companion users don’t need to do anything.
- **Tus error handlers:** check your` upload-error` code again, because` response` is now populated.


```text
-    import { fetcher } from '@uppy/utils'
+    import { fetcher } from '@uppy/core/utils'


-    import { RequestClient } from '@uppy/companion-client'
+    import { RequestClient } from '@uppy/core/companion-client'
```


` CompanionClientProvider` and` CompanionClientSearchProvider` are also gone. Import` Provider` from` @uppy/core/companion-client` in their place. The merge exists to prevent a specific failure: a lockfile holding an old copy of` @uppy/utils` next to a newer` @uppy/core` , which left two copies of the same package in one dependency tree.


Since Uppy 6.0,` @uppy/tus` passes the server’s status and response body to the` upload-error` event and to` file.response` . Earlier versions emitted the error without the server’s response.


```text
uppy  .  on  (  '  upload-error  '  , (  file  ,   error  ,   response  )   =>   {
if (  error  .  isNetworkError  )   return   showOfflineNotice  ();   // placeholder helper
console  .  log  (  response  ?.  status  );
console  .  log  (  response  ?.  body  .  xhr  .  responseText  );
});
```


You still get` undefined` for` response` in two cases: the server never replied (such as when it can’t be reached), or the file was a remote one uploaded through Companion.


## Using Uppy with React and Other Frameworks


Uppy’s framework wrappers let components subscribe to Uppy state without wiring up events by hand. In React, the` useUppyState` hook from` @uppy/react` takes an Uppy instance and a selector, and re-renders the component when the selected slice changes. The[React integration docs](https://uppy.io/docs/react/) describe the full API.


```text
import   {   useState   }   from   '  react  '  ;
import   Uppy   from   '  @uppy/core  '  ;
import   Tus   from   '  @uppy/tus  '  ;
import   {   useUppyState   }   from   '  @uppy/react  '  ;


function   UploadStatus  () {
const   [  uppy  ]   =   useState  (()   =>
new   Uppy  ().  use  (  Tus  , {   endpoint  :   '  https://your-tus-server/files/  '   }),
);
const   files   =   useUppyState  (  uppy  , (  state  )   =>   state  .  files  );
const   progress   =   useUppyState  (  uppy  , (  state  )   =>   state  .  totalProgress  );
return   <  p  >{Object  .  keys  (  files  ).  length} files, {progress}% uploaded</  p  >  ;
}
```


The lazy` useState` initialiser creates the Uppy instance once per component instead of on every render. Uppy also has wrappers for Vue, Svelte and Angular.


## When Not to Use Uppy


A single small file, such as a profile avatar, doesn’t need Uppy or Tus. A plain form POST to your own endpoint is enough, and Tus would add a server integration you then have to run. If you later want Uppy’s UI but keep a regular HTTP endpoint,[@uppy/xhr-upload](https://uppy.io/docs/xhr-upload/) covers that: it can send a standard multipart form upload or a` PUT` request. Our guide to[Multer file upload in Node](https://blog.openreplay.com/multer-npm-file-upload-nodejs/) shows the receiving side.


## Conclusion


Resumable uploads are why Uppy is worth adding. Uppy 6.0 makes it simpler to run, with one S3 plugin that has a single signing mode per configuration and one core package instead of five that had to stay in step. To start, install` @uppy/core` ,` @uppy/dashboard` and` @uppy/tus` , point the Tus plugin at a` tusd` instance, and upload a large file with your network throttled. If you’re already on 5.x, begin with the Companion and` upload-error` changes, since those are the ones that can break existing code.


## FAQs


What does the getCredentials function in @uppy/aws-s3 need to return?


It returns an object with a credentials property holding temporary credentials as camelCase accessKeyId, secretAccessKey and sessionToken, plus an optional expiration, and a region to sign for. AWS STS returns these keys in PascalCase, so map them first. Uppy caches the result for the plugin's lifetime. On an ExpiredToken or InvalidAccessKeyId error it fetches new credentials and retries once. Scope the attached policy tightly, because the browser holds these credentials.


Which @uppy/aws-s3 options were removed in Uppy 6.0, and does shouldUseMultipart still work?


shouldUseMultipart still works in @uppy/aws-s3 6.0, along with getChunkSize, allowedMetaFields and limit. The removed options are endpoint, headers, cookiesRule, getTemporarySecurityCredentials, getUploadParameters, signPart, createMultipartUpload, listParts, abortMultipartUpload, completeMultipartUpload, uploadPartBytes and retryDelays. Existing Companion setups migrate by renaming endpoint to companionEndpoint. headers and cookiesRule have no direct replacement: same-origin cookies still reach Companion, but bearer tokens or cross-site cookies need another setup, such as an authenticating proxy in front of Companion.


What is the difference between Tus resumable uploads and @uppy/golden-retriever?


Tus lets the server keep the bytes it already received so the transfer continues, while Golden Retriever restores the browser-side file selection and Uppy state after a crash or closed tab. In Uppy 6.0, Golden Retriever stores metadata, state and local files up to 10 MiB in IndexedDB by default, falling back to localStorage for metadata. Larger files need the optional Service Worker store, which survives closed tabs but not browser restarts.


Can an Uppy 6 client connect to an older Companion server?


No. An Uppy 6 client needs Companion 7, because OAuth tokens now travel over Companion's WebSocket connection instead of window.opener. Companion 7 keeps postMessage as a fallback for Uppy clients older than 6.0, so deploy Companion 7 first, then upgrade the client. On the server, pass companion.socket() the same options object you pass to companion.app(). Hosted Companion users need no changes.
